title: 2 Corinthians 5:11-13 – Persuading Men
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: Paul's defense against accusations from false apostles centers on his motivation to persuade all people of the gospel through fear of God and the love of Christ. The passage emphasizes that while the Holy Spirit alone saves, God uses believers' proclamation of Scripture to persuade people toward faith in Christ. The sermon contrasts Paul's commitment to biblical truth with the super apostles' focus on appearance and rhetoric.

outline.title: Understanding the Text: Context and Meaning of 2 Corinthians 5:11-13
subpoints: The word 'therefore' connects verse 11 to the judgment seat of Christ mentioned in verse 10
Paul's fear of the Lord motivates his aim to be well-pleasing to God, whether present or absent
The super apostles accused Paul of being crazy—unsophisticated in rhetoric and obsessed with the gospel
Paul responds that God knows his heart and approves of his commitment to Scripture alone

outline.title: Paul's Comparison with the Super Apostles
subpoints: The super apostles boasted in appearance and how people perceived them
Paul's boast was in pleasing the Lord, not in personal appearance or rhetorical skill
The Corinthians themselves knew Paul's message and could defend him against false accusations
Paul's confidence rested in the Corinthians' knowledge of his faithfulness to the gospel

outline.title: Application 1: Motivation by Fear and Love
subpoints: Paul persisted in gospel proclamation because he feared God and was controlled by Christ's love
The love of Christ destroys self-focus and directs attention toward others
Knowing Christ loves us brings freedom in faithful gospel proclamation despite criticism
Fear of the Lord and love of Christ work together as primary motivators for gospel ministry

outline.title: Application 2: Zeal for Persuading All People
subpoints: Paul had burning zeal to persuade all people of gospel truth
The Holy Spirit alone gives spiritual life, but uses believers' proclamation as the means
Romans 10:9-17 shows the logical progression: faith comes through hearing Scripture proclaimed
Paul consistently used Scripture-based arguments to persuade people to believe in Christ

outline.title: The Pattern of Paul's Persuasive Ministry in Acts
subpoints: Paul persuaded in the synagogue at Antioch using Scripture (Acts 13:15-41)
Paul addressed pagan worship in Lystra with biblical arguments (Acts 14:14-18)
Paul presented the gospel to the Philippian jailer from Scripture (Acts 16:30-34)
Paul reasoned in the Areopagus in Athens with biblical arguments (Acts 17:19-31)
Paul spent two years in Ephesus presenting persuasive arguments at the hall of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9-10)
Even in prison, Paul seized opportunities to present Scripture-based arguments for belief (Acts 22, 24, 26, 28)

outline.title: The Gospel as Power and the Necessity of Persuasion
subpoints: The gospel is God's power unto salvation—not a matter of personal power or skill
You cannot persuade others of what you are not persuaded of yourself
If you believe in Christ, you can articulate the gospel because it is propositional truth
The facts of the gospel are essential; belief and the ability to formulate truth are inseparable
The critical question is not ability but care: Do we care that people face judgment?

outline.title: The Challenge: Fear, Love, and Personal Sphere of Influence
subpoints: Every person will stand before the judgment seat of Christ
Only righteousness in Christ through faith can acquit us in judgment
Fear of God and love of Christ should compel us to share the gospel with those in our sphere
It is easy to share with strangers but difficult with those whose opinion matters—that tests our true belief
If we believe the gospel is God's power unto salvation, we will persuade all people

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are well known to God and I also trust are well known in your consciousness. For we do not command ourselves again to you, but give you opportunity to boast on our behalf that you may have an answer for those who boast in appearance and not in heart. For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God. Or if we are of sound mind, it is for you. For the love of Christ compels us because we judge thus that if one died for all, then all died. And he died for all that those who live should live no longer for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again. Therefore from now on, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh yet now we know him thus no longer. Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. Old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. Now all things are of God who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and has given us the ministry of reconciliation. That is, that God has in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their trespasses to them and has committed to us the word of reconciliation. Now then we are ambassadors for Christ as though God were pleading through us. We implore you on Christ's behalf be reconciled to God. For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

(2 Corinthians 5:11-21)

## Introduction

Have you ever heard the saying, "No good deed shall remain unpunished"? That seems to have been the motto of the Corinthian church toward the Apostle Paul. Not all of them, but a significant minority was always ready to listen to accusations against Paul and to entertain that those accusations were true.

Men whom Paul calls "super apostles" had come into the church and were trying to discredit his ministry. In 2 Corinthians 11:5, Paul says, "For I consider that I am not at all inferior to the most eminent apostles." The New King James says "eminent apostles," but if you look at the ESV, they have "super apostles." Paul is not praising these men. He is actually making fun of them—this idea that they think they're super apostles.

These men came into the church and tried to discredit his ministry. We already have found what they were saying twice in the first four or five chapters. In chapter two, Paul says that he is not like those men who peddle God's word, who minister God's word for profit, who change what the word of God says in order to gain more profit from the audience they are preaching to. And in chapter three, he says, "Look, I'm not like those people who you don't know and who need letters of recommendation. You Corinthians are my letters of recommendation. You have known me. You have been changed by the word that I proclaimed to you, not like the super apostles, the so-called super apostles, who need recommendations so that you can know who they are."

But these men came in and they were teaching things that were contrary to the gospel, contrary to Paul's teaching. And he goes back here in this passage to defend himself. And that's something that he's going to do throughout the letter of 2 Corinthians. He keeps on defending himself. But it's important that you notice that he defends himself not because he wants to look good in the minds or in the sight of the Corinthians. He's defending himself because these accusations against him were discrediting the gospel that he was preaching.

Now, we don't care as preachers or teachers what people say about us, as long as what is being said doesn't discredit the message. It makes sense? The person who stands up here is irrelevant. As long as the message of Christ is going forth and accusations are not discrediting that message, that's what matters.

I was surprised as I was preparing for this message to look at commentators and to see a great majority of the ones that I consulted saying that verses 11 through 21 is Paul's greatest declaration of the work of Christ in all of Scripture. You'd think that it would be somewhere in Romans or maybe in Ephesians, but they say this is the most concise and thorough declaration of the work of Christ in the gospel that we find in Paul's writings.

For us today, we're going to consider Paul's motivation for gospel proclamation and Paul's zeal for gospel proclamation. And then Lord willing next Lord's day in the afternoon, we're going to look at the effect of God's gospel proclamation.

## Part 1: Understanding the Text

### Verses 11-13: The Connection and Meaning

We're going to look at verses 11 through 13. So you don't have to be afraid—we read the whole, almost the whole chapter, but we're just going to look at verses 11, 12, and 13 for today.

If you look at your Bible in verse 11, you're going to find that the word "therefore" is there. For those who study Greek, you know that the word "therefore" is a post-positive word, which means it's never the first word of a sentence grammatically. And "therefore" tells us that verse 11 is connected with whatever comes before verse 11. So we have to figure out how that is connected.

Now, I'm not sure why the New King James translators started using the word "terror," saying "knowing therefore the terror of the Lord." Because the word is simply the word "fear," just like the expression that you find throughout the Bible: "the fear of the Lord." That's all that Paul is saying here—"knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, the reverence for the Lord, the awe of who God is and what he does, the desire to please him."

So knowing the fear of the Lord, Paul does something. The "therefore" links this fear of the Lord with previously mentioned truths. Paul is saying that knowing the fear of the Lord, he makes his aim, whether present or absent, to be well-pleasing to the Lord. That's why he says in verse 9 of the same chapter, "So that therefore it's connecting the fear of the Lord with our aim. If we fear God, we make our aim in life to please him, whether present or absent. We've seen that that means whether we're alive or dead.

But "therefore" also connects it with the idea of judgment that comes in verse 10. Knowing that every person will come before the judgment seat of Christ instills in Paul the fear of the Lord. And that should be true of all of us. Knowing that every person out here in verse 10 is designed for Christians—it is a judgment of reward—but it's true that every person who ever lived and whoever lives will stand before God and will give an account for what they have done in this life should instill a healthy fear of the Lord that propels us to proclaim the gospel so that they face that judgment in Christ, not on their own.

Because Paul knows that every person will come before the judgment seat of Christ to have all that was done in life judged in light of the law of God, he persuades people. Now, the basis of this judgment will be the law of God that's revealed in the Bible, that's revealed in all of creation, but it's also revealed in our hearts and our conscience. So he persuades people.

### What Does Paul Use to Persuade?

What is it he's using to persuade people? We said we're only going to look at verses 11, 12, and 13, but we are going to dip a little bit into verses 14 and 15. What is it that he persuades people with? The gospel of Jesus Christ. In verses 14 and 15, he says:

> For the love of Christ compels us because we judge thus that if one died for all, then all died and he died for all, that those who live should live no longer for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again.

That's what Paul is trying to persuade people of: that Christ died for sinners. And then when he rose back to life, he brought sinners back to life, and that love controls him as he goes forward.

### The Accusations Against Paul

Now it seems like the super apostles were making fun of Paul, and it was about two things—two aspects of his commitment to persuade people.

If you look at verse 13, Paul says, "If we are besides ourselves..." This seems to be the accusation that "Look, this guy is crazy. He's a madman. Look at how he talks." And the basis for that is that they said that Paul was unsophisticated in his rhetoric, that he did not speak like a well-trained Greek orator. Therefore, they made fun of him. Maybe he had an accent. He grew up speaking Hebrew, so maybe when he spoke in Greek he had an accent and people laughed at him because of it. Or he didn't use the proper rhetorical tools and terms and they said, "Why are you going to listen to that hillbilly guy? Look at him. Look at how he sounds."

And they made fun of him not only because he sounded funny, perhaps, or he didn't sound like they thought he would sound, but also because he insisted he only preached the Bible. Only crazy people do that, they said—that he sounded crazy with all this Bible talk.

And Paul says, "You know what? That's fine. I'm okay with being called crazy because God is okay with my sticking to the Bible and presenting the gospel through biblical arguments."

If you look at verse 11, he says, "Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are well known to God." He says, "Look, what's in me has been manifested and continues to be manifested before God. God is aware of what I'm doing, and the implication is that he's pleased with that. You want to think that I'm crazy because I stick to the Bible? You want to think that I'm crazy because I preach the gospel? You want to think I'm crazy because I don't try to sound like the wisdom of the world? Go right ahead. Do you know who thinks that I'm not crazy? God himself. So I'm happy," Paul says, "to continue that way."

The other thing that he has been accused of is that he was overly excited about the gospel. They were accusing him of acting like a crazy man because of his commitment to persuade people with the gospel of Jesus Christ. Can you imagine? "All this guy does is talk about Jesus. Can we talk about other things? There are other things out there that we should be talking about, but he only wants to talk about Jesus."

In 1 Corinthians 2, he says, "Look, the only thing I put before you is Christ and him crucified." They say, "He's a fanatic. He's a radical. He's a fundamentalist. Why are you going to listen to this crazy guy?"

Again, what does Paul say? "You know what? God is okay with me doing that. So I'm just going to keep on doing that."

And Paul was okay with that because of three things. As I said, his conscience was clear before God the Lord. It's that in verse 11. He was confident that the Corinthians themselves knew that he was being faithful to the Lord. He says that he knows that their consciences know that the accusations are false. The Corinthians know him. The Corinthians know his message. And they know that the accusations are false against him.

But also, Paul knows that obedience to God is often seen as irrational. But to those who have been changed by the Spirit, there's nothing more lucid, nothing more rational, nothing more reasonable than obedience to Christ.

And Paul continues by saying that he has been with the Corinthians enough for him not to have to justify himself again. In verse 12, he says:

> For we do not command ourselves again to you, but give you opportunity to boast on our behalf that you may have an answer for those who boast in appearance and not in heart.

As a matter of fact, the Corinthians have all the evidence they need to defend Paul against the accusations that the super apostles are making against him.

### Paul versus the Super Apostles

It is clear here that Paul is comparing his ministry with the ministry of these super apostles in this verse, because these super apostles were all about how they looked, how they sounded, and how they were accepted by the crowds. He says that they boast in their appearance. They boast in how people perceived them. That's not true. Not to get any picture of any current pastor in Houston for you, but think of someone with straight teeth, perfect hair, dressed in a tailored suit with the smile on his face. That's what mattered to them.

Paul knew, however, that to make his aim—to make his boast—anything other than pleasing the Lord is to boast in appearance instead of the heart. He says, "Corinthians, you know that my boast is not in my appearance. As a matter of fact, as I said before, we have one description of Paul that comes from the Second Century, from the 100s. And that description says that he was a balding man with a hooked nose, cross-eyed, and bowlegged. So he had definitely not boasted in his appearance."

We know that Paul was a bold man. We know that. And he wouldn't because what mattered for him was the heart of the message. And I hope that you see there that Paul is confident that the Corinthians knew that the heart of his message was the heart of the gospel. And I hope that you know about your own pastor that the heart of his message is the heart of the gospel.

## Part 2: Applications

### Application 1: Motivation by Fear and Love

Now that we understand what this passage means, let's consider how we should live in light of what Paul teaches us here. I have two broad applications with some specific applications under them. The first one is going to be shorter. The second one is going to be longer.

The first application from this passage is this: **We need to be motivated by fear and love in proclaiming the gospel.**

Paul keeps on ministering to the Corinthians and proclaiming the gospel to them because he fears God and because Christ loves him. So look at the beginning of verse 14. The translator says that the love of Christ "compels" us. That word "compels" can mean "controls." That might be a better translation. But the love of Christ—the love that Christ has for him—just pushes him, compels him, controls everything he does. And you find that in the heals in verse 11 where he's saying that the fear of the Lord also controls him.

Brothers and sisters, to keep going in gospel proclamation and in gospel life as a whole, we need to be convinced that God is worthy of our fear and that Jesus loves us.

Paul persuades all people in verse 11. "Persuades men"—"men" there is the general word for humanity. Paul persuades all people because he fears the Lord. And Paul is willing to come across as a madman, as a crazy guy, because the love that Christ has for him controls him.

More on this next week. But for now notice that the love that Christ has for us in verse 15 destroys self. The love that Christ has for us takes our eyes off of ourselves and puts us on other people. And if self no longer matters, who cares what critics of the gospel think or say about us?

Who cares?

> I've been crucified with Christ. And the life that I now live is not me living, but it's Christ living in me.

So who cares?

So you can see the freedom that knowing that Christ loves you brings in your faithful living and proclaiming the gospel of Jesus Christ.

We'll consider the love of Christ for us as a motivator more in future times. But the key point here is that fear and love motivate us to faithful gospel proclamation.

### Application 2: The Zeal for Persuading All Peoples

A longer application for us today is the zeal that Paul demonstrates in proclaiming the gospel. **Paul wanted to persuade all peoples of the truths of the gospel of Jesus Christ. There is a zeal in him for that.**

In verse 11, Paul's antimony state: "We persuade man." Have you ever stopped to think about this little clause, "We persuade man"? Have you ever stopped to think about what this short little clause means?

**It is only the Holy Spirit that persuades people. But he uses means to do so. And the means is us as we bear the word of God.**

Paul tells us that the spirit primarily uses the proclamation of the word of God to persuade people of the gospel of Jesus. Let me turn to Romans 10 to show you how Paul says that there, because it's a longer passage and it might be easier for you to follow, because we're going to look at how the spirit persuades but the spirit uses people proclaiming the gospel of Jesus Christ so that others might be changed. Romans 10, starting at verse 9:

> If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For the scriptures say, whoever believes on him will not be put to shame. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek for the same Lord over all is rich to all who call upon him. For whoever calls the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things." They have not all obeyed the gospel for Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report?" So then, faith comes by hearing and hearing by the word of God.

Do you get the point that Paul is making here? If you believe in the gospel, you will be saved. There's no question. We're not debating that. You will be saved. You are saved. You are being saved. You were saved. All those tenses are present here and all salvation is located outside of you, not in you. It is in Christ. It is your faith in what Christ has done and who he is that saves.

And Paul continues in verse 14, "How then shall they call on him in whom they shall not have believed?" So far he said, "It's Christ that saves. It's all Christ. It's all Christ. Christ is the one that changes. It's the spirit that changes people."

And then he says, "But there's means. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And then he continues this logical progression: "And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Now, "preacher" doesn't have to be a guy in a suit in front of the church. It can be you proclaiming the gospel to your friends and family.

We pray often for the unsaved family members, but if you pray and never share the gospel with them, you don't really believe that Jesus saves. The logical implication is that you don't really believe it.

Verse 15 continues: "And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things.'"

> They have not all obeyed the gospel for Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report?" So then, faith comes by hearing and hearing by the word of God.

Do you really have a fervor or a zeal for people coming to know Jesus? If you do truly, then you're sharing the word of God with them. Not a gimmick. Not some other thought. Not even your own story of salvation. As important as that might be, what saves is not your story. It's Christ's story. The spirit changes people, but he does that in response to persuasive arguments about the gospel.

And Paul firmly believed in both of these truths: We persuade. The spirit changes. We persuade. The spirit changes. And I hope you understand that the Holy Spirit is solely responsible for giving life to dead sinners.

Let me turn to one more passage. Ephesians chapter 2, verses 1 through 9, where clearly Paul teaches that the spirit is solely in charge of giving life to dead sinners:

> And you, being dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom also we all once conducted ourselves in the lust of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind and were by nature children of wrath, just as the others. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.

You, Christian, you members of the Ephesian church, you members of this church, you who believe in Jesus Christ—he made alive those who were dead in trespasses and sins. In which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience.

Among whom also we all once conducted ourselves in the lust of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind and were by nature children of wrath, just as the others. Who are these bad people, right here? I'm one of them. You were one of them.

But what happened? "But God." That's the key phrase. "But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses, made us alive together with Christ."

Billy Graham years ago wrote a book. I think the title was "What Must You Do to Be Born Again?" If that was written from a biblical perspective, you'd open and page one would be blank, page two would be blank, page three would be blank. And as you go on, because according to this passage, you dead people don't do anything to come to life. It is God who brings us to life. Dead people don't do anything to come to life. It is God who brings you to life.

Yet, yet—Paul took hold of every opportunity to present a persuasive argument from the Bible, explaining why people should believe in Jesus Christ.

It is the spirit that changes people. And yet he uses means—uses persuasive arguments. How that works is a mystery, but that's how he does it. People are born again as a result of the proclamation of the word, but that action is not their action. It's the spirit's action in changing their hearts.

### Paul's Pattern of Gospel Persuasion Throughout Acts

If you just work your way through the book of Acts, when Paul comes to prominence in chapter 8 and 9, there's a bit of hiatus. They go back to emphasizing Peter. But then in chapter 13, Paul becomes the main character in the book of Acts.

In Acts 13:15-41, Paul finds himself in the synagogue in Pisidia Antioch, somewhere in Turkey. And what does he do? He persuades them to believe in Jesus.

In Acts 14:14-18, now he's in Lystra. No synagogue. There's a bunch of people trying to worship him as Hermes and Barnabas as Zeus. And what does he do? What would the super apostles have done? They would say, "Oh man, they think we're great people." No. Paul and Barnabas, they tear their clothes off and stop: "Stop, don't do that." And then he presents the persuasive argument why the pagans should believe in Jesus.

In Acts 16:30-34, he and Silas are in jail singing hymns at midnight. An opportunity to present the gospel appears. Guess what Paul does? He presents a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why the Philippian jailer should believe.

In Acts 17:1-3, he goes to the synagogue in Thessalonica. And for three Sabbaths presents a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why the Jews should believe.

Then in Acts 17:19-31, he finds himself in the marketplace in Athens, in the Areopagus, with all the learned of the town. And guess what he does? He presents a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why they should believe.

In Acts 19:8, he finds himself in the synagogue in Ephesus. He's a rabbi in town—a new rabbi in town—and they say, "Oh, come and tell us something." Guess what he does? He presents a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why they should believe in Christ.

In Acts 19:9-10, we're told that for two years he rented the school of Tyrannus, the hall of Tyrannus, at noon to present a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why people should believe in Jesus Christ.

In Acts 22:1-21, he's beaten in the temple. People think he's bringing Gentiles. The Romans shackle him. They drag him off the stairs. He says, "Sir, in flawless Greek: Sir, may I talk to this crowd that wants to kill me just for a minute?" And guess what he does? He presents a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why they should believe in Jesus Christ.

In Acts 24:10-21, he's before Felix while in prison in Caesarea Philippi. Felix says, "What do you want to talk about? Why should I let you go?" Paul says, "Forget that. I don't care about going or not. But let me present you a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why you should believe in Jesus Christ."

Acts 26:1-23: Now before Festus and Herod Agrippa, still in prison in Caesarea. Herod says, "Oh man, I heard this Paul. I'd love to hear him talk. Maybe he can even do a miracle here for us." And Paul says, "Forget that. Let me make you, let me make a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why you should believe in Jesus Christ." The point is so compelling that Herod says, "Stop, stop, because you're almost making me believe in him."

In Acts 28:23-29, while in jail in house arrest in Rome, Jews come to him and say, "What do you have to tell us? Good question. Let me make a persuasive argument from the Scriptures why you should believe in Jesus Christ."

The point I'm making: The guy who wrote, literally wrote the book on the Spirit being the one that changes people, is also the guy that the book says spent his time persuading people to believe in Jesus Christ. I just gave you eleven examples from the book of Acts alone in which Paul is working to persuade people by using biblical arguments explaining why people should believe in Jesus Christ.

Why in the world would he do that? Have you ever thought about that? Why in the world would he do that?

Well, because Paul knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation. And he says that in Romans chapter 1: "For I'm not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes."

And if you are believing Jesus Christ, but you doubt your salvation, what you're saying is that you are more powerful than the Holy Spirit, which is idolatrous, because the gospel you believe is the power of God unto salvation.

## Part 3: The Critical Application

Brothers and sisters, this is the key. You cannot persuade others of what you are not persuaded yourself. You can try, but if you're not persuaded of the gospel of Jesus Christ, you cannot persuade others.

Paul says this in 2 Timothy 1:12:

> For this reason, I also suffer these things. Nevertheless, I am not ashamed for I know whom I have believed. And I'm persuaded that he is able to keep what I've committed to him until that day.

If you're a believer in Jesus Christ, you know the gospel. And we are persuaded this is true. If you're a believer in Jesus Christ, you are also able to formulate the truth of the gospel. You're able to tell others what that gospel is because the gospel is a set of propositional truths—statements with a theological implication. And if you're not, if you don't know the facts of the gospel, you cannot believe in Jesus Christ.

It's simpler than it is clear that while it is possible to formulate the truth of the gospel and not believe in it, it is not possible to believe in it and not be able to formulate the truth.

"Oh pastor, I don't tell us about Jesus because I just don't know what to say." If you don't know what to say, you don't know whom you believe either. And that's very important to keep in mind.

## Part 4: The Challenge

Do we get that every person in the world will stand before the judgment seat of Christ and will give an account for all that was done in this life? Do we get that the only way to be acquitted, to be declared not guilty on that day, is to come clothed in the righteousness of Christ by faith alone?

Perhaps a more valid question—perhaps actually a more applicable question is this: **Do we care?**

That's why that's where the zeal comes in. Are we motivated by our fear of God because he's worthy of our fear? And are we motivated by the love of God that controls us to proclaim the gospel of Jesus Christ to everyone we see, especially the people in our sphere of influence?

It's really easy to share the gospel with a stranger, right? But are you sharing the gospel with those people whose opinion you care about because you've been made a fool in their sight? Do you believe that the gospel of Jesus Christ is God's power unto salvation for all peoples? If it is, then you persuade all people because you know that he is faithful and he will keep what you committed to him until the day of his coming.
